paras: The Sixth and Broadway street fight was a brief clash in Paducah, Kentucky, on the late afternoon of 22 May 1903, in which a number of white people joined a fight between white and Black boys and drove off the Black boys and a Black cyclist who had come to their aid. No one was reported hurt, and the only known account is a short item in the Paducah Sun that treated the affair as one of two "lively altercations" without bloodshed.

According to the Sun, some white and "colored" boys were fighting at the corner of Sixth and Broadway when a Black man on a bicycle came along and, seeing that the white boys were winning, "butted in." A number of white people then arrived and "also took a hand in the controversy," and the paper reported that "in a short time the negroes were hard to find." The item gives no names, no number for the white crowd, and no account of weapons or injuries.

The mother of the Black boys reached the scene during the trouble and threatened to get warrants, but the Sun said she "failed to do it." No report of arrests, charges or court proceedings appears in the coverage.

The Paducah Sun ran the story on 23 May 1903 under the headline "Lively Altercations but in Neither Was There Any Bloodshed," pairing it with a quarrel between a streetcar conductor and a passenger returning from a baseball game. Its tone was light: it cast the Black cyclist as the one who "butted in" and reported the flight of the Black participants as the end of the matter. No other white paper and no Black paper is known to have reported the fight.

accounts.gist: The Paducah Sun told the story lightly: a Black cyclist 'butted in' on a boys' fight the whites were winning, white people joined in, and the Black participants were soon 'hard to find'.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Lively Altercations but in Neither Was There Any Bloodshed', the Sun treated the fight as street excitement, said the cyclist 'butted in', and noted the mother 'failed' to get warrants.
